screens.title: Monitoring & Auditing Security with CloudTrail, CloudWatch, & AWS Config
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on three complementary AWS services that together form a practical security monitoring and auditing stack. CloudTrail records the who, what, and when of all A P I activity, giving you an immutable audit trail of actions across your account. CloudWatch Logs takes those event records and lets you search, filter, and convert patterns into metrics and alarms for real-time detection. AWS Config continuously snapshots resource configurations and evaluates them against rules you define so you can enforce compliance over time. You will learn why each service matters, how they integrate, and a step-by-step example: creating a CloudTrail trail that delivers to a centralized S3 bucket and CloudWatch Logs, adding a CloudWatch Metric Filter and Alarm to detect root account activity, and enabling an AWS Config managed rule for S3 server-side encryption. A layered strategy uses CloudTrail for forensic evidence, CloudWatch for fast detection and notification, and Config for continuous posture checks. By the end, you will understand both the controls to enable and the practical trade-offs — for example, broad data events can be high volume so record management matters — and you will be ready to design a monitoring plan that keeps logs immutable, alarms actionable, and compliance automated. Which event would you monitor first in your environment?

screens.title: AWS CloudTrail — What it records and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: CloudTrail is the authoritative record of A P I activity in your AWS account. It logs management events — who called which A P I, from where, and when — whether the call comes from the console, SDKs, CLI, or another AWS service. A clear example is an S3 bucket policy change: CloudTrail records which principal made the change, the time, and the request parameters. That record is vital for forensic analysis after a security incident and for regulatory audits that require a persistent trail. A common misconception is that the console shows a complete history; the console displays recent management events by default, but only a configured CloudTrail trail delivers consistent logs to durable storage. For long-term retention and immutability, deliver trails to an S3 bucket with KMS encryption and enable log file validation. Also enable multi-region logging to ensure events in every region are captured; an attacker could attempt activity in an unused region if you only record a single region. Key practical considerations include choosing which event types to record: management events are low-volume and essential; data events such as S3 object-level operations are high-volume and should be enabled selectively for specific forensic needs. Takeaway: treat CloudTrail as your canonical audit record and centralize it to a secured, separate account for resilience.

keyIdea.title: CloudTrail definition
keyIdea.text: CloudTrail records API activity across the account; centralize logs to S3, enable KMS encryption and log validation for audit integrity.

content.html:
Core Concept

What CloudTrail records

CloudTrail logs management API calls and can deliver those records to S3 for durable retention. Decide between management and data events based on forensic needs.

Recorded fields
  • Who (user, role)
  • What (API name and parameters)
  • When (timestamp)
  • Where (source IP, region)
Common misconception

The console's recent events are not a substitute for a centralized trail; configure a trail for consistent, long-term logs.

Practical example

If an S3 bucket policy is changed, CloudTrail captures the API call and the principal, and that record is used in investigations and audits.

Key Takeaway

CloudTrail is your canonical audit log. Centralize, encrypt, and validate logs to maintain forensic integrity.

Trail configuration cards
Centralized S3

Create a trail that delivers logs to a centralized S3 bucket in a dedicated logging account; enable versioning and lifecycle rules for retention.

KMS & validation

Enable SSE-KMS for log files and log file validation to detect tampering; keep keys and access separate from the producer account.

Event selection

Record management events by default; enable data events like S3 object access only where necessary due to volume and cost.

Why this matters

Immutable, centralized logs allow you to reconstruct actions, support legal discovery, and demonstrate compliance to auditors. Without centralization and encryption, attackers can attempt to erase traces.

screens.title: Create a CloudTrail trail to S3 and CloudWatch Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a CloudTrail trail is a repeatable, low-risk configuration that transforms ephemeral console views into durable audit evidence. Start by choosing a descriptive trail name, for example MySecurityTrail, then configure the storage location: create or designate an S3 bucket and enable server-side encryption with a KMS key. Enable log file validation so CloudTrail publishes digests that help detect tampering. Next, enable CloudWatch Logs integration by supplying a log group name and an IAM role for CloudTrail to write logs. Select management events (read and write) as the baseline; only enable data events selectively because they increase cost and volume. For multi-account environments, centralize logs into a dedicated logging account and enable multi-region logging so events in all regions are captured. A common configuration mistake is granting overly broad permissions to the S3 bucket or KMS key; follow least privilege and ensure the logging role can write but cannot delete the KMS key or the S3 bucket. Finally, wait a few minutes for the trail to become active and verify that initial events appear in S3 and CloudWatch Logs. This process provides a hardened foundation for both detection and forensics.

keyIdea.title: Setup guidance
keyIdea.text: Configure a trail with S3 + KMS encryption, log file validation, CloudWatch Logs integration, and multi-region delivery for durable, tamper-resistant auditing.

content.html:
Process Flow

Create CloudTrail trail

1
Name and scope
Choose a trail name and enable for all regions to capture global activity.
2
S3 and KMS
Create a dedicated S3 bucket, enable SSE-KMS encryption, and enable log file validation.
3
CloudWatch Logs
Enable CloudWatch Logs integration and supply a log group and IAM role for delivery.
4
Event selection
Record management events by default. Only enable data events where necessary.
Common mistake

Giving write and delete access on the S3 bucket to too many principals. Keep write limited to the CloudTrail delivery role.

Verification card

After creating the trail, verify three things:

  1. Objects appear in the S3 bucket and are encrypted with SSE-KMS.
  2. CloudWatch Logs receives events in the specified log group.
  3. Trail status shows Active and multi-region delivery is enabled if selected.
Example IAM role note

Create a narrowly scoped IAM role for CloudTrail to write to CloudWatch Logs and S3, and avoid using wide admin permissions for delivery operations.

screens.title: Integrate CloudTrail with CloudWatch Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Delivering CloudTrail events to CloudWatch Logs allows you to convert audit records into metrics and alarms for near real-time detection. Once a trail is configured to send to CloudWatch Logs, the next step is to define metric filters. A metric filter inspects incoming JSON event records for a pattern you care about, such as failed ConsoleLogin or specific A P I calls that modify IAM or network configurations. When a filter matches, it emits a metric datapoint that you can use with a CloudWatch Alarm. An illustrative pattern is detecting ConsoleLogin failures by searching for ConsoleLogin events where errorMessage indicates a failed login. Important practical notes: craft patterns to balance sensitivity and noise — overly broad patterns create alert fatigue, whereas overly narrow patterns can miss subtle attacks. Also be aware of log latency: CloudWatch delivery is near real-time but not instantaneous; design thresholds and notification workflows accordingly. Finally, ensure the log group and metric namespace use consistent naming so your team can find and maintain filters easily. This integration is the bridge from raw audit data to actionable alerts.

keyIdea.title: Why integrate
keyIdea.text: CloudWatch Logs enables searching and metric conversion of CloudTrail events so you can detect and respond to security signals quickly.

content.html:
Process Flow

CloudTrail → CloudWatch Logs

Send events to a CloudWatch Log Group and then create Metric Filters to turn specific log patterns into metrics.

Filter design tips
  • Start with a focused pattern for high-signal events.
  • Test patterns against recent logs to validate matches.
  • Use namespaces and clear names for metrics and filters.
Why this matters

Converting logs to metrics enables fast alarms and integrations with notification services for rapid incident response.

Concrete example

Metric Filter pattern to detect failed ConsoleLogin events (example):

{ ($.eventName = "ConsoleLogin") && ($.errorMessage = "*") }

This filter emits a metric each time a ConsoleLogin event contains an error message indicating a failed login attempt.

Operational note

Tune the pattern to reduce false positives, for example by excluding known automation accounts or certain regions if appropriate.

screens.title: CloudWatch Metric Filters and Alarms
screens.narratorSegment: Metric Filters are rules you add to a CloudWatch Log Group that count or extract values from matching log events and publish them as metrics. Once you have a metric, you can attach a CloudWatch Alarm that triggers when the metric crosses a threshold. Imagine you want to be alerted when there are more than five failed login attempts in five minutes: the metric filter increases a counter for each failed ConsoleLogin, and an alarm watches the Sum statistic over a five-minute period and notifies an SNS topic if the count exceeds five. This approach is straightforward, but there are important design considerations. Choose metric thresholds that balance sensitivity with operational noise. Use dimensions and namespaces to organize metrics so that team owners can manage thresholds per account or environment. For notification, SNS topics are the common glue — subscribe email endpoints, pager integrations, or ticketing systems. A frequent misconception is that creating too many alarms improves security; however, excessive alarms lead to alert fatigue and ignored signals. Prioritize high-fidelity events tied to meaningful actions like root activity, policy changes, or network access modifications, and include playbooks so alerts lead to consistent response actions.

keyIdea.title: Alerting pattern
keyIdea.text: Metric Filters convert logs to numeric signals; CloudWatch Alarms watch those signals and notify via SNS for response orchestration.

content.html:
Comparison

Metric Filters vs Alarms

Metric Filters create metrics from patterns. Alarms act on those metrics and trigger actions when thresholds cross.

  • Metric Filter: pattern → metric datapoint
  • Alarm: metric → threshold → action (SNS)
Best practice

Group alarms by severity and routing: critical alarms to paging, informational alarms to dashboards or ticketing.

Example alarm setup
  1. Create a Metric Filter named FailedConsoleLogin in the CloudTrail log group.
  2. Publish metric to namespace CloudTrailMetrics with metric name FailedLoginCount and value 1 per match.
  3. Create an Alarm on FailedLoginCount: period 5 minutes, statistic Sum, threshold >= 5.
  4. Attach an SNS topic named SecurityAlerts to notify the on-call team.
Key Takeaway

Alarms translate log patterns into operational actions; tune thresholds and routes to keep alerts actionable.

screens.title: Root Account Activity — Filter pattern and alarm
screens.narratorSegment: Detecting root account activity is a high-priority security control because root use is rare and often indicates an emergency or misuse. A reliable approach is to create a CloudWatch Metric Filter that looks for userIdentity. type equal to Root and userName equal to root, while excluding AWS service events. The provided filter pattern does exactly that and maps each match to a metric named RootLoginCount. Once the metric exists, create an alarm that triggers on any occurrence within a short window — for example, a five-minute period with Sum greater than or equal to one. The practical test is simple: after subscribing an email to the SNS topic, log out and sign in using the root credentials; the alarm should enter an alarm state and send the notification. A common misconception is that root activity always implies compromise. Root use can be legitimate for bill/payment tasks, but because it is high-risk, it must be monitored and guarded by strong controls such as MFA and minimal daily use. Closing question: how would you adjust notifications so approved root tasks do not create pager noise but still provide audit evidence?

keyIdea.title: Root detection
keyIdea.text: Use a focused metric filter that counts root user activity and an alarm that notifies immediately; test by performing a controlled root login.

content.html:
Definition

Root Account Alarm

Create a metric filter that identifies events where the root user performed an API call and use an alarm to notify your team immediately.

Metric Filter pattern
{ ($.userIdentity.type = "Root") && ($.userIdentity.userName = "root") && ($.eventType != "AwsServiceEvent") }

This pattern counts any management event executed by the root principal while ignoring automated AWS service events.

Alarm configuration
  • Metric namespace: CloudTrailMetrics
  • Metric name: RootLoginCount
  • Period: 5 minutes, Statistic: Sum
  • Threshold: Greater or equal to 1 → Notify SNS topic
Test and operationalize

To test: create an SNS topic called SecurityAlerts, subscribe an email endpoint, confirm the subscription, then log in as root to trigger the metric filter and alarm. Verify the alarm state and the received email.

Misconception

Root activity always means compromise. Not always — sometimes root is used for legitimate billing tasks — but it should be rare, monitored, and accompanied by MFA and approval processes.

Key Takeaway

Root account usage is high-risk and should be both minimized and immediately visible through alarms and notifications.

screens.title: AWS Config — Continuous configuration monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config continuously captures the configuration state of your AWS resources and records changes over time. It is designed for posture management and compliance, not for logging A P I calls. You enable AWS Config to record all resources or a targeted set, and it builds a historical inventory that auditors and engineers can query. The power of AWS Config is in rules: managed rules or custom rules evaluate recorded configurations against a desired state. For example, a managed rule named s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled verifies that S3 buckets have server-side encryption enabled; when a noncompliant resource is detected, Config marks it as noncompliant. You can optionally trigger automated remediation when a rule fails, such as applying an automation runbook to enable encryption. A key contrast with CloudTrail: CloudTrail answers who did what, while AWS Config answers whether resources meet policy and how they have drifted over time. Use both together: CloudTrail can point to the actor who changed a resource while Config shows the resulting misconfiguration and history. Remember that Config generates data and evaluation costs; scope it thoughtfully and use managed rules when possible to reduce custom development.

keyIdea.title: Config purpose
keyIdea.text: AWS Config tracks resource configuration history and evaluates compliance with rules to prevent drift and demonstrate posture over time.

content.html:
Definition

AWS Config explained

Config records resource configurations over time and evaluates them against rules to detect drift and noncompliance.

Config Records

Snapshots of resource settings and relationships, stored for auditing and query.

Rules

Managed or custom rules evaluate whether resources meet policies such as encryption, tagging, or network restrictions.

Remediation

Config can trigger automated remediation when a rule becomes noncompliant, reducing manual effort to correct drift.

Concrete example

Enable the managed rule s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled to check that newly created buckets are encrypted. When a bucket is not encrypted, Config marks it noncompliant and can launch a Systems Manager Automation document to apply encryption.

Misconception

Config is not a replacement for CloudTrail. Use CloudTrail for activity logs and Config for desired-state checks.

Key Takeaway

Config provides continuous visibility into resource state and enforces policy through rules and remediation.

screens.title: Enable AWS Config and add S3 encryption rule
screens.narratorSegment: Enabling AWS Config is straightforward but requires deliberate choices. Start by enabling recording for all resources if you need broad visibility, or scope to resource types that matter to your compliance goals. Create or choose an S3 bucket where Config will deliver snapshots and select an IAM role for Config to use. After Config is recording, add managed rules rather than immediately creating custom rules — managed rules cover many common security and compliance checks and reduce maintenance overhead. A concrete, high-value rule is s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled. Add that rule and allow Config time to evaluate existing resources; noncompliant buckets will appear in the Rules dashboard. If you want automatic fixes, attach a remediation action such as an AWS Systems Manager Automation document to the rule so the system attempts to correct noncompliance. Watch out for costs and evaluation frequency: recording many resource types at a high evaluation cadence increases charges. Finally, validate by creating an unencrypted S3 bucket and observing it transition to noncompliant, which confirms both recording and rule evaluation are functioning. Enable AWS Config and add S3 encryption rule means record resources, add managed rules like s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled, and optionally attach automated remediation for continuous compliance.. In practical terms, turn on recording and add the managed rule for s3 server-side encryption.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process

Enable AWS Config

  1. Open AWS Config and choose to record all resources or a subset.
  2. Create a new S3 bucket for Config snapshots and choose or create the Config IAM role.
  3. Add managed rules, for example s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled.
  4. Optionally attach remediation to automatically correct issues.
Operational tip

Start with managed rules and expand to custom rules only when necessary. Monitor rule evaluations and cost impact as you scale recording.

Validation example

After enabling the s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled rule, create a new S3 bucket without encryption. Within minutes, Config should mark it Noncompliant and list the resource in the rule's details. This verifies both recording and evaluation.

Key Takeaway

Use managed rules for common checks and attach remediation to reduce manual effort when drift occurs.

screens.title: Design a layered monitoring and auditing strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A robust security posture combines three layers: evidence, detection, and enforcement. CloudTrail provides the evidence by recording A P I activity across your accounts and regions. CloudWatch converts that evidence into signals through Metric Filters and Alarms so your operations team can detect and respond in near real-time. AWS Config enforces the desired state by continuously evaluating resource settings against rules and optionally remediating noncompliance. In practice, design a central logging account to receive CloudTrail S3 deliveries and enable multi-region trails to avoid gaps. Route CloudWatch alarms to SNS topics that integrate with your incident management system. Use Config Rules to cover high-impact policies like encryption, public access, and required tags. An example flow: CloudTrail logs an AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress call; a CloudWatch Metric Filter detects that the rule opened SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 and raises an alarm; AWS Config flags the security group as noncompliant if it violates a rule, and an automated remediation closes the port. This layered approach ensures you have both the who/what history and the automated gates to return systems to policy quickly. Think in terms of complementary capabilities rather than single-point solutions.

content.html:
Architecture

Layered monitoring strategy

Combine centralized audit logs, metric-based detection, and continuous configuration checks for resilient security operations.

Evidence

CloudTrail to S3 with KMS and log validation — durable, central, and auditable.

Detection

CloudWatch Logs → Metric Filters → Alarms → SNS for rapid notifications and playbook-triggered responses.

Enforcement

AWS Config rules to detect drift and optionally trigger automated remediation to restore policy compliance.

Scenario walkthrough

Example sequence: CloudTrail logs an AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0. A CloudWatch Metric Filter flags the API call and an Alarm alerts the security team. Simultaneously, an AWS Config Rule that prohibits unrestricted SSH marks the security group noncompliant and a remediation runbook closes the port. CloudTrail preserves the who/when for post-incident analysis.

Operational checklist
  • Centralize logs to a dedicated account
  • Protect log storage with KMS and access controls
  • Tune metric filters for high signal
  • Automate remediation for common drift

screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on sequence follows the exact steps you need to practice the core configurations. First, create a CloudTrail trail named MySecurityTrail. Create or select an S3 bucket for log delivery, enable SSE-KMS encryption, and turn on log file validation. Enable CloudWatch Logs delivery and allow CloudTrail to create a new IAM role for delivery. Next, create an SNS topic called SecurityAlerts and subscribe an email endpoint, confirming the subscription via the confirmation email. This lab gives you verifiable checks at each stage and ties auditability, alerting, and compliance into a single workflow.

Hands-on Activity

Step-by-step checklist

  1. Create CloudTrail trail MySecurityTrail with S3 delivery, SSE-KMS, and log file validation.
  2. Enable CloudWatch Logs delivery with a new log group CloudTrail/MySecurityTrailLogs and delivery IAM role.

Metric Filter (root detection)

screens.title: CloudTrail vs CloudWatch vs AWS Config — Roles and differences
screens.narratorSegment: It is essential to understand the distinct roles of each service so you apply them correctly. CloudTrail records A P I activity and is the source of truth for who did what and when; store those logs in S3 for durable audits. CloudWatch focuses on observability and near real-time reactions: ingest logs, define metric filters, and raise alarms to notify or drive automated responses. AWS Config is focused on state and compliance: it records resource configurations and evaluates them against rules to enforce desired state. A concrete juxtaposition: if an IAM policy is changed, CloudTrail tells you which principal performed the change and with what parameters; CloudWatch can alert if you configure a metric filter for the specific A P I call; and AWS Config can evaluate whether the resulting policy violates any compliance rules and flag or remediate it. A common operational error is relying on a single service: for example, using Config alone for detection will miss timing-sensitive events, while relying solely on CloudWatch alarms without centralized CloudTrail means you lack a durable forensic record. Use them together to get auditability, detection speed, and continuous policy enforcement.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on three complementary AWS services that together form a practical security monitoring and auditing stack. CloudTrail records the who, what, and when of all A P I activity, giving you an immutable audit trail of actions across your account. CloudWatch Logs takes those event records and lets you search, filter, and convert patterns into metrics and alarms for real-time detection. AWS Config continuously snapshots resource configurations and evaluates them against rules you define so you can enforce compliance over time. You will learn why each service matters, how they integrate, and a step-by-step example: creating a CloudTrail trail that delivers to a centralized S3 bucket and CloudWatch Logs, adding a CloudWatch Metric Filter and Alarm to detect root account activity, and enabling an AWS Config managed rule for S3 server-side encryption. A layered strategy uses CloudTrail for forensic evidence, CloudWatch for fast detection and notification, and Config for continuous posture checks. By the end, you will understand both the controls to enable and the practical trade-offs — for example, broad data events can be high volume so record management matters — and you will be ready to design a monitoring plan that keeps logs immutable, alarms actionable, and compliance automated. Which event would you monitor first in your environment?

By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain the purpose of CloudTrail, configure a trail that delivers logs to a secure S3 bucket and CloudWatch Logs, construct CloudWatch Metric Filters and Alarms to detect security events, and use AWS Config Rules to continuously validate resource configuration. Each objective links a capability to why it matters: logs without retention are not useful for audits, alarms without context create noise, and compliance rules without automation allow drift. For example, you will not just enable CloudTrail; you will configure it for all regions and centralize logs to a dedicated account so an attacker cannot erase evidence easily. You will build a CloudWatch metric filter that counts root account activity and wire that metric to an SNS topic for immediate notification. You will also enable a managed AWS Config rule to check for unencrypted S3 buckets and observe how noncompliant resources appear. These skills let you move from reactive troubleshooting to proactive detection and continuous enforcement. Which objective will you tackle first in your own environment?

This second objectives screen ties skills to scenarios you will practice. You will configure a CloudTrail trail that delivers management events to S3 and CloudWatch Logs, choosing encryption and log validation for tamper-resistance. You will create an SNS topic and subscription for notifications and test a CloudWatch Alarm by triggering root account activity. You will also enable AWS Config recording and add the managed rule that checks for server-side encryption on S3 buckets. Each objective includes a short verification step: confirm that CloudTrail appears in the destination S3 bucket with KMS-encrypted logs, verify that the CloudWatch alarm enters an alarm state when the test event occurs, and inspect AWS Config for rule compliance state changes. These practical checks convert configuration actions into verifiable evidence for audits and help you build confidence that alerts and compliance detections are working as expected. As you work, remember that data events like S3 object-level logging can be costly and high-volume; choose what to record based on forensic needs.

CloudTrail is the authoritative record of A P I activity in your AWS account. It logs management events — who called which A P I, from where, and when — whether the call comes from the console, SDKs, CLI, or another AWS service. A clear example is an S3 bucket policy change: CloudTrail records which principal made the change, the time, and the request parameters. That record is vital for forensic analysis after a security incident and for regulatory audits that require a persistent trail. A common misconception is that the console shows a complete history; the console displays recent management events by default, but only a configured CloudTrail trail delivers consistent logs to durable storage. For long-term retention and immutability, deliver trails to an S3 bucket with KMS encryption and enable log file validation. Also enable multi-region logging to ensure events in every region are captured; an attacker could attempt activity in an unused region if you only record a single region. Key practical considerations include choosing which event types to record: management events are low-volume and essential; data events such as S3 object-level operations are high-volume and should be enabled selectively for specific forensic needs. Takeaway: treat CloudTrail as your canonical audit record and centralize it to a secured, separate account for resilience.

Creating a CloudTrail trail is a repeatable, low-risk configuration that transforms ephemeral console views into durable audit evidence. Start by choosing a descriptive trail name, for example MySecurityTrail, then configure the storage location: create or designate an S3 bucket and enable server-side encryption with a KMS key. Enable log file validation so CloudTrail publishes digests that help detect tampering. Next, enable CloudWatch Logs integration by supplying a log group name and an IAM role for CloudTrail to write logs. Select management events (read and write) as the baseline; only enable data events selectively because they increase cost and volume. For multi-account environments, centralize logs into a dedicated logging account and enable multi-region logging so events in all regions are captured. A common configuration mistake is granting overly broad permissions to the S3 bucket or KMS key; follow least privilege and ensure the logging role can write but cannot delete the KMS key or the S3 bucket. Finally, wait a few minutes for the trail to become active and verify that initial events appear in S3 and CloudWatch Logs. This process provides a hardened foundation for both detection and forensics.

Delivering CloudTrail events to CloudWatch Logs allows you to convert audit records into metrics and alarms for near real-time detection. Once a trail is configured to send to CloudWatch Logs, the next step is to define metric filters. A metric filter inspects incoming JSON event records for a pattern you care about, such as failed ConsoleLogin or specific A P I calls that modify IAM or network configurations. When a filter matches, it emits a metric datapoint that you can use with a CloudWatch Alarm. An illustrative pattern is detecting ConsoleLogin failures by searching for ConsoleLogin events where errorMessage indicates a failed login. Important practical notes: craft patterns to balance sensitivity and noise — overly broad patterns create alert fatigue, whereas overly narrow patterns can miss subtle attacks. Also be aware of log latency: CloudWatch delivery is near real-time but not instantaneous; design thresholds and notification workflows accordingly. Finally, ensure the log group and metric namespace use consistent naming so your team can find and maintain filters easily. This integration is the bridge from raw audit data to actionable alerts.

Metric Filters are rules you add to a CloudWatch Log Group that count or extract values from matching log events and publish them as metrics. Once you have a metric, you can attach a CloudWatch Alarm that triggers when the metric crosses a threshold. Imagine you want to be alerted when there are more than five failed login attempts in five minutes: the metric filter increases a counter for each failed ConsoleLogin, and an alarm watches the Sum statistic over a five-minute period and notifies an SNS topic if the count exceeds five. This approach is straightforward, but there are important design considerations. Choose metric thresholds that balance sensitivity with operational noise. Use dimensions and namespaces to organize metrics so that team owners can manage thresholds per account or environment. For notification, SNS topics are the common glue — subscribe email endpoints, pager integrations, or ticketing systems. A frequent misconception is that creating too many alarms improves security; however, excessive alarms lead to alert fatigue and ignored signals. Prioritize high-fidelity events tied to meaningful actions like root activity, policy changes, or network access modifications, and include playbooks so alerts lead to consistent response actions.

Detecting root account activity is a high-priority security control because root use is rare and often indicates an emergency or misuse. A reliable approach is to create a CloudWatch Metric Filter that looks for userIdentity. type equal to Root and userName equal to root, while excluding AWS service events. The provided filter pattern does exactly that and maps each match to a metric named RootLoginCount. Once the metric exists, create an alarm that triggers on any occurrence within a short window — for example, a five-minute period with Sum greater than or equal to one. The practical test is simple: after subscribing an email to the SNS topic, log out and sign in using the root credentials; the alarm should enter an alarm state and send the notification. A common misconception is that root activity always implies compromise. Root use can be legitimate for bill/payment tasks, but because it is high-risk, it must be monitored and guarded by strong controls such as MFA and minimal daily use. Closing question: how would you adjust notifications so approved root tasks do not create pager noise but still provide audit evidence?

AWS Config continuously captures the configuration state of your AWS resources and records changes over time. It is designed for posture management and compliance, not for logging A P I calls. You enable AWS Config to record all resources or a targeted set, and it builds a historical inventory that auditors and engineers can query. The power of AWS Config is in rules: managed rules or custom rules evaluate recorded configurations against a desired state. For example, a managed rule named s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled verifies that S3 buckets have server-side encryption enabled; when a noncompliant resource is detected, Config marks it as noncompliant. You can optionally trigger automated remediation when a rule fails, such as applying an automation runbook to enable encryption. A key contrast with CloudTrail: CloudTrail answers who did what, while AWS Config answers whether resources meet policy and how they have drifted over time. Use both together: CloudTrail can point to the actor who changed a resource while Config shows the resulting misconfiguration and history. Remember that Config generates data and evaluation costs; scope it thoughtfully and use managed rules when possible to reduce custom development.

Use them together to get auditability, detection speed, and continuous policy enforcement.
